name: InterviewIQ
tagline: AI mock interviews: it generates questions from a role or job description, listens to your answers, and grades them.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Interview prep tools are a thin wrapper around three primitives that are now commodities: a prompt that generates plausible questions, speech to text, and a rubric prompt that scores your answer. None of that is proprietary, and there is no network on the other side of the app that you need. The one honest advantage a paid tool has is a curated bank of real, role-specific questions and feedback tuned by someone who has read a lot of bad answers, and a personal build will feel more generic on both counts. But for the actual job of rehearsing out loud and hearing something specific back, a local build gets you most of the way in one sitting. You will pay an LLM provider a few cents per session instead of a subscription.
coreLoopDIY: Paste a job description, get a question set, record spoken answers in the browser, and get a transcript plus rubric-scored feedback stored locally so you can see improvement over sessions.
requirements: An OpenAI or Anthropic API key (plus a speech to text endpoint) in .env
Node 20 and local disk for the SQLite file
whatYouLose: A curated bank of real questions asked by specific companies, versus whatever the model invents
Feedback rubrics that were tuned against thousands of actual answers, not your first guess at a prompt
Polish: pacing, timers, filler-word detection, video framing, all the things that make a mock feel like an interview
A mobile app and any progress tracking that follows you off your laptop
Someone else maintaining it when the speech model or API changes under you
moatNotes: The only durable asset here is a question corpus tied to real roles and companies, plus whatever feedback data comes from watching users fail. Everything visible on the surface is prompt engineering.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because job hunting is a high-stakes, short-duration panic, and nobody wants to spend the Saturday before an onsite debugging their own microphone permissions. A paid tool is also implicitly a promise that the questions resemble the real thing, which matters more than the software when you are nervous. Twenty or thirty dollars for a month of prep is trivially justified against a salary bump, so the willingness to pay is enormous and the switching cost is zero. That is a good business, not a hard technical moat.
notes: The entire category exists because interview anxiety makes people reach for a credit card, not because the code is difficult.
prompt:
Build a local-only AI mock interview trainer. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, and better-sqlite3 writing to ./data/app.db. Run with `npm run dev` on port 3000. Nothing else.

Secrets: read OPENAI_API_KEY from .env.local. Provide .env.example. Fail with a clear message if it is missing.

Core flow:
1. Setup page: textarea for a job description or role title, dropdown for interview type (behavioral, technical screen, hiring manager), and a question count (5 to 10).
2. On submit, call the model server-side to generate that many questions as strict JSON. Store the session and questions in SQLite.
3. Interview page: show one question at a time with a visible elapsed timer. Record audio in the browser with MediaRecorder, upload the blob to an API route, transcribe it with the OpenAI transcription endpoint, and save the transcript against the question.
4. After each answer, score it server-side against a fixed rubric: specificity, structure (STAR for behavioral), relevance to the job description, and filler-word density computed from the transcript. Return a 1 to 5 per axis, one concrete rewrite suggestion, and one thing that was actually good.
5. Session report page: all questions, transcripts, scores, and a per-axis average. Sessions list page ordered by date so progress is visible.

Explicitly in scope: audio recording, transcription, rubric scoring, SQLite history, export a session to Markdown.
Explicitly out of scope: video, real-time interruption, voice synthesis of an interviewer, resume parsing, auth, payments, multi-user, deployment config.

Keep prompts in a single src/lib/prompts.ts file with the rubric as an editable string, so tuning does not mean hunting through route handlers. Handle microphone permission denial and transcription failures with visible errors, not silent no-ops. Write a README with setup in under ten lines.
